We have mass spec giving m/z 179.0946 (intensity 100). Likely molecular ion M+? The formula we derived from isomers list: C10H13NO2 has exact mass? Let's calculate: C10 = 120.000, H13 = 13.101, N = 14.00307, O2 = 31.9898. Sum = 179.094 approx. Yes matches. So molecular formula C10H13NO2.

Proton NMR shows signals: 2.58 (t, 2H), 2.84 (t, 2H) suggests ethylene chain CH2-CH2 attached to something (maybe aromatic). 3.81 (s, 3H) methoxy. Aromatic: 7.17 ddd 2H, 7.93 ddd 2H suggests para-disubstituted benzene (AA'BB') pattern. So aromatic ring with two substituents para to each other. The methoxy likely on aromatic (anisole). The other substituent is amide? The pattern of two CH2 groups suggests maybe -CH2-CH2- attached to amide nitrogen? Actually N-CH2-CH2- attached to aromatic? Let's examine candidate SMILES from isomers list that matches N-CH2-CH2- aromatic and methoxy para.

First candidate: 'CC1=C(C(=CC=C1)OC)NC(=O)C' This is: a benzene with methoxy (OC) at position? Let's parse: CC1=C(C(=CC=C1)OC)NC(=O)C. That is a methyl (C) attached to aromatic carbon? Actually "CC1=" indicates a methyl attached to aromatic carbon (i.e., a tolyl). The ring: C1= C( C(=CC=C1)OC ) N C(=O)C. So we have a para? Not sure. Contains methoxy (OC) and an amide (NC(=O)C) attached to ring. No ethyl chain CH2-CH2. So not match.

Second: 'COC1=CC2=C(C[C@@H]([C@@H]2N)O)C=C1' This is a benzodioxane? Contains OCH3? Actually COC1=... has methoxy attached to aromatic, plus a fused ring with CH-CH(N)O. Not match.

Third: 'CC(=O)NC(=O)C/C=C\\\\C=C/C=C' Not aromatic.

Fourth: 'CC1=C2C(=CC=C1)C(C(CO2)O)N' This is maybe indoline? Not.

We need aromatic para-disubstituted with methoxy and something that gives CH2-CH2 (two equivalent CH2 groups). Could be -CH2-CH2- attached to N (i.e., N-CH2-CH2- attached to aromatic? Actually N attached to aromatic (anilide) and N attached to ethyl chain? But N is part of amide? The N is attached to carbonyl (amide) and aromatic. The ethyl chain could be part of carbonyl side chain: e.g., acetamide? But CH2-CH2 suggests maybe -CH2-CH2-CO-? Wait the NMR shows two triplets each 2H, typical for -CH2-CH2- attached to aromatic on one side and carbonyl on other? For example, phenethyl amide? Actually phenethyl amide would be -CH2-CH2- attached to aromatic (CH2 next to aromatic appears ~2.7) and CH2 next to carbonyl appears ~2.3. Here both at 2.58 and 2.84, plausible.

So structure: para-methoxy phenyl attached to amide of phenethyl? Let's think: 4-methoxy phenyl attached to carbonyl of something? The N is attached to carbonyl (amide) and to ethyl chain? Wait we have amide: -C(=O)NH-CH2-CH2-? Actually NMR shows two CH2 triplets, likely -CH2-CH2- attached to N (i.e., N-CH2-CH2-). But N-CH2-CH2- would have N attached to CH2 (alpha) and CH2 attached to something else (maybe carbonyl). However the carbonyl is attached to N, not to CH2. So maybe the chain is -CH2-CH2- attached to aromatic (phenethyl) and carbonyl attached to N? Actually phenethyl amide: aromatic-CH2-CH2-CO-NH-? That would give CH2 next to aromatic ~2.7 (triplet) and CH2 next to carbonyl ~2.3 (triplet). But our NMR shows both around 2.6-2.8, okay.

But we also have methoxy on aromatic. So maybe 4-methoxy phenethyl amide? The amide carbonyl attached to N? Wait phenethyl amide would be phenethyl attached to carbonyl (C=O) attached to N? Actually phenethyl amide is phenethyl attached to carbonyl (C=O) which is attached to N (i.e., phenethyl-CO-NH-). That would give CH2 next to carbonyl (alpha to carbonyl) ~2.3, not 2.8. But okay.

Alternatively, maybe the structure is 4-methoxy phenylacetanilide? That is p-anisidine acetamide: p-anisidine (4-methoxy aniline) attached to acetamide (NH-CO-CH3). That would have CH3 (singlet) not CH2-CH2. So not.

Our NMR shows 3.81 (s, 3H) methoxy. Aromatic 4 protons as AA'BB' pattern (para-disubstituted). So ring has two substituents para. One is methoxy. The other is something that gives ethyl chain CH2-CH2 attached to carbonyl? Could be -CH2-CH2-CO-? Actually if substituent is -CH2-CH2-CO-NH-? That would be para-ethyl amide? But then the carbonyl is not attached to ring directly, but via ethyl chain. The NMR would show CH2 next to aromatic (2.7) and CH2 next to carbonyl (2.3). The carbonyl carbon not observed in 1H. The amide NH maybe not seen.

Our formula C10H13NO2 includes only one carbonyl O (C=O) and one O in methoxy. So total O2. So carbonyl present. The methoxy O is OCH3. So the carbonyl is part of amide (C=O). So we have an amide group attached to aromatic via ethyl chain? That would add extra carbons: aromatic ring (6 C), methoxy adds 1 C, ethyl chain adds 2 C, carbonyl carbon adds 1 C = total 10 C. Yes matches C10. Hydrogens: aromatic 4 H (para-disubstituted), methoxy 3 H, ethyl chain 4 H, amide NH 1 H = total 12? Wait formula says H13. Let's count: aromatic 4 H, methoxy 3 H =7, ethyl CH2-CH2 =4 H =>11, amide NH =1 =>12, plus maybe carbonyl carbon has no H. That's 12. Need 13. Maybe there is an extra CH3 somewhere? But we have only 10 carbons accounted: 6 aromatic, 1 methoxy carbon, 2 ethyl, 1 carbonyl =10. Hydrogens: aromatic 4, methoxy 3, ethyl 4, amide NH 1 =12. So missing one hydrogen. Could be that the amide is N-CH (i.e., secondary amide with N attached to CH3? But we have only 10 carbons, can't have extra CH3. Maybe the amide nitrogen is not protonated (i.e., tertiary amide) and we have extra hydrogen elsewhere? Actually formula C10H13NO2 includes 13 H, so there is one extra H beyond our count. Could be that the aromatic ring is not para-disubstituted but ortho? But pattern suggests AA'BB'.

Maybe the chain is -CH2-CH2- attached to N (i.e., N-CH2-CH2- attached to aromatic? That would give N-CH2 (2H) and CH2 attached to something else (maybe carbonyl). But we need carbonyl O. Could be N-CH2-CH2-CO-? That would be N attached to CH2 (2H) and carbonyl attached to CH2 (2H). That matches two triplets. The aromatic substituent is attached to carbonyl (i.e., aromatic-CO-CH2-CH2-NH-). That would be para-methoxy phenyl carbonyl attached to ethyl amide. That is p-anisoyl ethyl amide? Actually structure: p-anisoyl ethyl amide = p-methoxybenzoyl ethyl amide (i.e., p-anisoyl ethyl amide). SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCC. Let's check: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCC. Count carbons: CO (methoxy) adds 1 C, aromatic 6, carbonyl carbon 1, ethyl chain 2 =10. Hydrogens: methoxy 3, aromatic 4, ethyl 4, amide NH 1 =12. Still 12. Wait formula would be C10H13NO2? Let's compute: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCC. The amide nitrogen attached to ethyl (CH2CH3) not CH2CH2? Actually N-CH2-CH3 gives CH3 (3H) and CH2 (2H). But our NMR shows two triplets each 2H, not a quartet+triplet. So ethyl is CH2-CH3, not CH2-CH2. So not match.

Our NMR shows two triplets each 2H, typical for -CH2-CH2- where both ends are attached to heteroatoms (N and aromatic). So chain is -CH2-CH2- between aromatic and N? That would be phenethyl amide? Actually phenethyl amide: aromatic-CH2-CH2-CO-NH-? That gives CH2 next to aromatic (2H) and CH2 next to carbonyl (2H). Both appear as triplets. So structure: p-methoxy phenethyl amide? That is p-anisyl-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2? Wait carbonyl attached to NH2, not N attached to chain. The chain is attached to aromatic, carbonyl attached to NH2. So SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N. Count: aromatic 6, methoxy carbon 1, CH2-CH2 (2), carbonyl carbon 1 =10. Hydrogens: aromatic 4, methoxy 3, CH2-CH2 4, NH2 2 =13. Yes matches formula C10H13NO2. NMR: we would see NH2 maybe broad, not reported. The two CH2 triplets match. Aromatic AA'BB' pattern matches para-methoxy phenyl. So this fits perfectly.

Thus SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N. Let's verify formula: Use get_formula.
